findings.title: Money requested before any viewing
findings.detail: The agent asks for money before you have seen the property in person. Paying before a viewing is the most common way students lose a deposit.

evidence.quote: Please transfer GBP 700 to another account now;

findings.title: Overpayment and refund request
findings.detail: Paying more than is owed and refunding the difference is a known scam pattern: the original payment bounces or is reversed after you send the refund. The agent claims money was sent by mistake and asks you to send some on. This is a well-known fake overpayment scam, and a screenshot is not proof that any money arrived.

evidence.quote: My accountant accidentally sent you GBP 2000. Please transfer GBP 700 to another account now; the screenshot proves it arrived.

questions: Have you viewed the flat in person, and have you been asked to pay anything for it so far?
Did you receive any actual money in your account, or only the screenshot?

findings.title: Deposit is within the amount cap
findings.detail: This amount check does not verify deposit protection or authenticity. Annual rent GBP 15600; cap = 15600 / 52 * 5 (GBP 1500.00 rounded down to pennies); requested GBP 1500. Importance: 85/100. Conditional: Confirm that the rented property is in England. Confirm this is an ordinary private tenancy, not an excluded arrangement. Confirm that rent and deposit cover the same whole tenancy. The cap arithmetic holds on the quoted figures: rent of GBP 1300 per calendar month gives annual rent of GBP 15,600. Five weeks is 15,600 / 52 * 5 = GBP 1,500, and the stated deposit of GBP 1,500 is exactly at the cap, not above it. This is a correctly limited amount-cap pass and I am not overturning the calculation. It is conditional because the context leaves the jurisdiction ("unknown"), the tenancy type ("unknown") and the rent basis ("unknown") unresolved. The rule applies only to covered tenancies, and nothing in the contract confirms the property is in England, that this is an ordinary private tenancy, or that rent and deposit cover the same whole tenancy. The address is in London, but that does not settle coverage. The result says nothing about deposit protection or authenticity. Nothing in the contract defeats the issue, so it should not be dismissed. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/tenant-fees-act-2019-guidance-for-tenants

findings.title: Credibility you cannot check
findings.detail: This presents a screenshot as proof, but a screenshot cannot show cleared funds in your own account; the plain version is that the agent says the money arrived. This is an order that discourages you from using the one party who could confirm what happened; the plain version is that the agent does not want your bank involved.
